title: ADHD and Sleep: Why You Can’t Just “Go to Bed Earlier”

The ADHD brain often struggles with delayed sleep phase. The internal clock or circadian rhythm tends to be shifted later than average. Melatonin does not rise when it should, so even when the body is exhausted, the brain might not feel sleepy until very late. Add low dopamine, difficulty transitioning, and mental overstimulation, and bedtime can become a real challenge. For many people with ADHD, that second wind at night is not random: it is the brain finally getting space to decompress after a long day of masking or structure. It is not about laziness or poor discipline; it is about brain chemistry, nervous-system regulation, and transitions. Four strategies can help. First, get natural light early in the morning, within 30–60 minutes of waking. This anchors the circadian rhythm and helps melatonin rise at the right time later. Second, use a reverse alarm 60–90 minutes before bed to begin transitioning. The ADHD brain struggles with abrupt stops, so this creates space to shift out of hyperfocus gradually. Third, reduce nighttime decision-making by keeping a consistent, predetermined wind-down routine. Fewer choices mean less friction and smoother transitions into rest. Fourth, schedule downtime earlier.
